overview.title: Inspecting the RoBERTa backbone
overview.main_topic: What a KerasHub backbone is, and the structure and size of RoBERTa-base as shown by backbone.summary()
overview.central_idea: A backbone is a pretrained model not yet specialized for a task: RoBERTa-base maps token ids (plus a padding mask) to a (batch_size, sequence_length, 768) sequence of contextual vectors using an embedding layer and 12 stacked TransformerEncoder layers, 124 million parameters in total. A task head is attached next.
overview.importance: This is the largest model in the book so far. Reading its summary, and being able to rebuild every parameter count from the architecture, ties the pretrained model back to the encoder block built in section 15.3.2.
learning_objectives: Define a backbone and explain why it has no loss function attached
Read the RoBERTa backbone summary: inputs, embeddings, layer norm, dropout and 12 encoder layers
Derive the embedding (38,996,736) and per-encoder-layer (7,087,872) parameter counts from vocabulary size, sequence length, hidden size 768 and feedforward size 3072
Compare RoBERTa-base's scale to the 14M-parameter translation Transformer
prerequisites: The TransformerEncoder block (pp.468-469) and positional embeddings (p.475)

paragraphs.excerpt: a backbone refers to any pretrained model that is not yet specialized for
paragraphs.what_it_says: In KerasHub, a backbone is any pretrained model not yet specialized for a task. The loaded model embeds an input sequence into an output sequence of shape (batch_size, sequence_length, 768) but has no loss function. It could be used for many downstream tasks: sentence classification, identifying text spans, part-of-speech tagging, and so on.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The output keeps the sequence axis, so you get one vector per token, and each vector depends on the entire sequence through bidirectional self-attention. Different tasks use this tensor differently. Sentence classification pools it, for example by taking the first (`<s>`) token's vector. Span extraction and part-of-speech tagging make a prediction at every position.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Because the output is per-token and general, one pretraining run can serve a whole family of tasks. The task-specific part is a small head on top.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: 768 is RoBERTa-base's hidden size. With 12 attention heads, each head works in a 768/12 = 64-dimensional subspace.

terminology.meaning: The specific supervised task a pretrained model is adapted to after pretraining.
Predicting which contiguous range of tokens contains some information (for example, the answer to a question).
Labeling each token as noun, verb, adjective and so on; a per-token classification task.

connections: p.480: the definition starts with the chapter 8 computer-vision meaning of 'backbone'
p.479: the encoder is bidirectional, which is what makes these representations rich

paragraphs.excerpt: Next, we will attach a classification head to this backbone that specializes it
paragraphs.what_it_says: The next step attaches a classification head that specializes the backbone for IMDb review classification. The authors compare this to fitting different heads to a screwdriver, a Phillips head for one task and a flat head for another.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The head is a small network, typically a Dense layer (possibly with dropout), that maps the backbone's features to class probabilities. Fine-tuning then trains the head and, usually, the whole backbone with a small learning rate.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the backbone + head pattern used throughout KerasHub, and it is the same idea as using a pretrained convnet base with a new classifier in computer vision.

terminology.meaning: Task-specific output layers placed on top of a backbone to produce class predictions.
Continuing to train a pretrained model, or part of it, on a downstream task's labeled data.

connections: p.484: section 15.4.4 fine-tunes the backbone with the attached head

paragraphs.excerpt: Let’s take a look at our backbone. We loaded the smallest variant of RoBERTa
paragraphs.what_it_says: (Second printed paragraph within this element.) Although this is the smallest RoBERTa variant, it has 124 million parameters, the biggest model used in the book so far. The summary follows.
paragraphs.what_it_means: 'Smallest' is relative: RoBERTa-large has about 355M parameters (not stated in the book). Compared with the book's earlier models, 124M is large: the translation Transformer had 14.4M (p.474), and the BERT paragraph on p.479 gives a range of 100M to 300M.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: At 473 MB of float32 weights, plus gradients and optimizer state for training, fine-tuning this model needs a proper GPU. That shapes the batch size and sequence length choices on the following pages.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: training with Adam stores weights, gradients and two moment estimates, roughly 4 × 473 MB ≈ 1.9 GB before activations, and activations for 512-token sequences add considerably more.

terminology.meaning: A size configuration of the same model family (for example, base or large).

connections: p.474: the translation Transformer summary shows 14,428,824 parameters
p.479: BERT was trained in sizes from 100 million to 300 million parameters

paragraphs.what_it_says: The summary of `roberta_backbone`: InputLayer `token_ids` (None, None); `embeddings` (TokenAndPositionEmbedding) (None, None, 768) with 38,996,736 parameters; `embeddings_layer_norm` with 1,536; `embeddings_dropout` with 0; InputLayer `padding_mask` (None, None); then `transformer_layer_0` to `transformer_layer_11`, each a TransformerEncoder with 7,087,872 parameters, connected to the previous layer and to `padding_mask`. Total 124,052,736 parameters (473.22 MB), all trainable.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The sequence length is `None` because the model accepts any length up to its position-embedding limit. Every encoder layer reads the padding mask, so attention ignores `<pad>` positions. The model is almost exactly the stack you would get by repeating the chapter's `TransformerEncoder` 12 times on top of a token-plus-position embedding.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Every number can be derived from four hyperparameters (vocabulary 50,265, max positions 512, hidden 768, feedforward 3,072). Doing so checks that you understand where a Transformer's parameters live: about 31% in embeddings and about 69% in the encoder stack.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: embeddings = 50,265×768 + 512×768 = 38,603,520 + 393,216 = 38,996,736. Encoder layer = attention 4(768²+768) = 2,362,368 + FFN (768·3072+3072) + (3072·768+768) = 4,722,432 + two layer norms 2·1,536 = 3,072, giving 7,087,872. Total = 38,996,736 + 1,536 + 12×7,087,872 = 124,052,736. Memory = 124,052,736 × 4 bytes = 473.22 MiB. The vocabulary size implied by the embedding count, 50,265, matches the 'only a 50,000-term vocabulary' on p.480 after rounding.

terminology.meaning: A KerasHub layer that sums a token embedding and a learned position embedding, like the chapter's PositionalEmbedding layer.
A boolean input that marks real tokens (True) versus padding (False), so attention skips pads.
Normalizes each token's vector over its features, with a learned scale and offset (2 × 768 parameters).

connections: p.469: the TransformerEncoder layer with self-attention, two Dense layers and two LayerNormalizations
p.475: positional embeddings, whose learned position table appears here inside 'embeddings'
p.483: StartEndPacker produces exactly the token_ids and padding_mask inputs listed here

paragraphs.excerpt: RoBERTa uses 12 Transformer encoder layers stacked on top of each other.
paragraphs.what_it_says: RoBERTa stacks 12 Transformer encoder layers, a big step up from the translation model.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Depth lets the model build increasingly abstract contextual representations, with each layer attending over the previous layer's outputs. The translation model had one encoder block (and one decoder block) at width 256. RoBERTa-base has 12 blocks at width 768, and each block alone has about 7M parameters.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows the scaling that pretraining makes possible: an architecture you already know, made deeper and wider and trained on 160 GB of text.

terminology.meaning: Feeding the output of one encoder block as the input of the next, with identical input and output shapes.

connections: p.473: Listing 15.16 builds the translation Transformer with hidden_dim = 256 and a single encoder and decoder block

concepts.name: Backbone
concepts.definition: In KerasHub, any pretrained model that is not yet specialized for a task: it maps inputs to latent features and has no loss or output head.
concepts.intuition: It is the handle of a screwdriver; you click on whichever head the job needs.
concepts.technical: The RoBERTa backbone takes `token_ids` and `padding_mask`, both (batch, seq_len), and returns (batch, seq_len, 768).
concepts.significance: One expensive pretraining run serves many cheap downstream tasks.
concepts.example: The same RoBERTa backbone can serve sentence classification, span identification or POS tagging.
concepts.misconception: That a backbone outputs one vector per sentence. It outputs one vector per token, and pooling is the head's job.

concepts.name: Classification head
concepts.definition: Task-specific layers attached on top of a backbone to produce class predictions.
concepts.intuition: It is the Phillips or flat head in the screwdriver analogy.
concepts.technical: It usually pools the per-token features (for example, takes the first token) and applies Dense layers with a softmax or sigmoid output.
concepts.significance: It is the only part that has to be trained from scratch for a new task.
concepts.example: A 2-class head for IMDb positive/negative reviews.
concepts.misconception: That only the head is trained during fine-tuning. Often the whole backbone is updated too, with a small learning rate.

concepts.name: Stacked Transformer encoder
concepts.definition: A deep network made of identical encoder blocks (self-attention plus feedforward, with residuals and layer norm) applied one after another.
concepts.intuition: Each layer refines every token's representation by looking at all the other tokens again.
concepts.technical: RoBERTa-base: 12 layers, hidden size 768, feedforward size 3,072, 12 heads; 7,087,872 parameters per layer.
concepts.significance: Depth and width together with pretraining data give the representational power that made BERT-style models state of the art.
concepts.example: transformer_layer_0 to transformer_layer_11 in the summary.
concepts.misconception: That RoBERTa uses a different kind of block from the one built in this chapter. The book says the internals almost exactly match.

concepts.name: Where a Transformer's parameters live
concepts.definition: The breakdown of model size between embedding tables and the encoder stack.
concepts.intuition: The vocabulary lookup table is a big one-off cost; each extra layer adds a fixed amount.
concepts.technical: Embeddings scale with (vocab + max_positions) × d; each layer scales with roughly 12d² (4d² for attention, 8d² for an FFN with 4d inner width).
concepts.significance: It explains why subword vocabularies are kept around 50k and how adding layers grows the model.
concepts.example: $12 \times 768^2 = 7{,}077{,}888$, close to the printed 7,087,872; the difference is biases and layer norms.
concepts.misconception: That most parameters are in attention. In each block the feedforward network has twice as many as attention.

math.title: Embedding parameters

variables.meaning: Vocabulary size (50,265 for RoBERTa's BPE; about 50,000 in the book's wording)

math.operations: A token table of shape (V, d) plus a position table of shape (L_max, d), summed per token.
math.purpose: Explains the largest single entry in the summary.
math.interpretation: About 31% of RoBERTa-base is lookup tables.
math.intuition: Each vocabulary entry and each position owns one 768-dimensional vector.

math.title: Parameters of one TransformerEncoder layer
math.latex: \begin{aligned} P_{\text{layer}} &= \underbrace{4(d^2+d)}_{\text{Q,K,V,O}} + \underbrace{(d f + f) + (f d + d)}_{\text{feedforward}} + \underbrace{2\cdot 2d}_{\text{2 LayerNorms}} \\ &= 2{,}362{,}368 + 4{,}722{,}432 + 3{,}072 = 7{,}087{,}872 \end{aligned}

variables.meaning: Feedforward (intermediate) size, 3,072 = 4d (RoBERTa-base config, not printed in the book)

math.operations: Four d×d projections with biases for multi-head attention, a two-layer feedforward network d→f→d, and two layer norms with a scale and an offset each.
math.purpose: Confirms the printed per-layer count and shows where the parameters are.
math.interpretation: The feedforward network has twice as many parameters as attention.
math.intuition: Splitting into heads doesn't change the count: 12 heads of size 64 together form a 768×768 projection.

math.title: Total parameters and memory

variables.meaning: Bytes in float32 (4 bytes per parameter)

math.operations: Sum of the embedding, embedding layer norm and 12 identical encoder layers; multiply by 4 bytes and divide by $2^{20}$.
math.interpretation: Keras prints MiB but labels it 'MB'.
math.intuition: Twelve copies of a 7M block plus a 39M lookup table.

code.title: Summary of the RoBERTa-base backbone
code.what_it_does: Prints the layer-by-layer structure of the RoBERTa-base backbone loaded in Listing 15.20: names, types, output shapes, parameter counts and connections.

line_explanations.explanation: Calls `summary()` on the functional Keras model named "roberta_backbone".
`token_ids` input, shape (None, None): any batch size and any sequence length.
`embeddings`: token plus learned position embeddings, giving (None, None, 768). It has 38,996,736 parameters (50,265×768 + 512×768).
LayerNormalization over the embeddings (scale and offset, 2×768 = 1,536 parameters), then Dropout (no parameters).
Second input, `padding_mask`, fed to every encoder layer.
12 TransformerEncoder layers (0, 1, ..., 11; layers 2-10 elided as '...'), each with 7,087,872 parameters, each taking the previous output and the padding mask.
124,052,736 parameters in total, all trainable; 473.22 MiB in float32.

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: token_ids (batch, seq_len) int and padding_mask (batch, seq_len) bool. Output: (batch, seq_len, 768) float features.
code.algorithm: Embed tokens and positions, normalize, apply dropout, then 12 rounds of masked bidirectional self-attention plus feedforward.
code.theory_link: It is the bidirectional encoder of BERT/RoBERTa (p.479) and matches the TransformerEncoder of section 15.3.2.

parameters.name: padding_mask
parameters.role: Stops attention from looking at padding tokens.

pitfalls: Both inputs are required; feeding only token_ids raises an error or lets attention look at padding.
Sequence length is None but limited to 512 by the position table, so longer inputs must be truncated (StartEndPacker does this on p.483).
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written check, not from the book: reproduce the summary numbers
V, L, d, f, n_layers = 50265, 512, 768, 3072, 12
emb = V * d + L * d                               # 38,996,736
ln = 2 * d                                        # 1,536
layer = 4 * (d * d + d) + (d * f + f) + (f * d + d) + 2 * (2 * d)  # 7,087,872
total = emb + ln + n_layers * layer               # 124,052,736
print(emb, layer, total, total * 4 / 2**20)       # ... 473.22

deeper.title: Rebuilding the summary by hand
deeper.body:
| Component | Formula | Count |
|---|---|---|
| Token embeddings | 50,265 × 768 | 38,603,520 |
| Position embeddings | 512 × 768 | 393,216 |
| Embedding LayerNorm | 2 × 768 | 1,536 |
| Attention (Q, K, V, O) per layer | 4 × (768² + 768) | 2,362,368 |
| Feedforward per layer | 768·3072+3072 + 3072·768+768 | 4,722,432 |
| Two LayerNorms per layer | 4 × 768 | 3,072 |
| **Per layer** | | **7,087,872** |
| **12 layers** | | **85,054,464** |
| **Total** | | **124,052,736** |

The vocabulary 50,265 and feedforward 3,072 are RoBERTa-base config values, not given in the book; they are the values that reproduce its printed counts exactly.

deeper.title: Translation Transformer vs. RoBERTa-base
deeper.body:
- Translation model (pp.473-474): hidden 256, one encoder block and one decoder block, **14.4M** parameters, trained from scratch in this chapter.
- RoBERTa-base: hidden 768, 12 encoder blocks, **124M** parameters, pretrained on 160 GB of text (p.479).

Per-layer cost grows with $d^2$: going from width 256 to 768 makes each block about 9 times larger, and there are 12 of them.

deeper.title: One backbone, many heads
deeper.body:
The three tasks the page lists use the (batch, seq_len, 768) output in different ways:

- **Sentence classification**: take the vector at `<s>` (or average over tokens) and apply Dense with softmax.
- **Span identification**: apply Dense(2) at every position to score each token as a span start or end.
- **Part-of-speech tagging**: apply Dense(num_tags) with softmax at every position.

The backbone is unchanged in all three; only the head and the loss differ.

misconceptions.claim: The backbone outputs a single vector per review.
misconceptions.correction: It outputs (batch_size, sequence_length, 768), one vector per token. Reducing that to one vector is the head's job.

misconceptions.claim: Most of a Transformer's parameters are in the attention layers.
misconceptions.correction: In each RoBERTa layer the feedforward network has 4.72M parameters against 2.36M for attention, and the embeddings account for about 39M of the total.

misconceptions.claim: 'Smallest variant' means RoBERTa-base is a small model.
misconceptions.correction: At 124M parameters it is the biggest model in the book so far, nearly nine times the 14.4M translation Transformer.

misconceptions.claim: A backbone already knows the IMDb task.
misconceptions.correction: It is not set up for any loss function; it needs a head and fine-tuning.

takeaways: In KerasHub, a backbone is a pretrained model not yet specialized for a task; it outputs per-token features (batch, seq_len, 768) and has no loss.
A task head (here, an IMDb classifier) is attached on top, like interchangeable screwdriver heads.
RoBERTa-base is token and position embeddings plus 12 TransformerEncoder layers, with 124,052,736 parameters (473 MB).
Each encoder layer has 7,087,872 parameters: about 2.36M in attention, 4.72M in the feedforward network, and 3K in layer norms.
Every encoder layer receives the padding mask so that attention ignores padding tokens.

questions.question: What is the output shape of the RoBERTa backbone?
questions.explanation: p481_e03 states this shape: one 768-d vector per token. (batch, 768) would need pooling, (batch, 2) is a classifier output, and (batch, seq, vocab) would be a masked-LM head.

questions.question: Verify the per-layer count 7,087,872 given hidden size 768 and feedforward size 3,072.
questions.explanation: Multi-head attention has query, key, value and output projections, each d×d plus bias. The FFN has two Dense layers, and each LayerNorm has a scale and an offset of size d.

questions.question: Using the summary, check that the total is 124,052,736 and that it occupies about 473 MB in float32.
questions.explanation: Dropout and the inputs have no parameters. Keras' 'MB' divides by 2^20.

questions.question: Why does every transformer_layer in the summary connect to padding_mask?
questions.answer: Each layer's self-attention must ignore padding positions, so the mask is passed to every layer, not only the first.
questions.explanation: Padding tokens are added to reach a fixed length (p.482-483). Without the mask, real tokens would attend to padding at every layer.

questions.question: What does the screwdriver analogy describe?
questions.answer: A single backbone fitted with different task-specific heads (for example, a classification head for IMDb), as you fit different heads to one screwdriver.
questions.explanation: p481_e04: Phillips head for one task, flat head for another.

questions.question: Which part of RoBERTa-base has the most parameters?
questions.explanation: 12 × 7.09M = 85.1M, against 39.0M for the embeddings. The layer norm has 1,536 parameters and the inputs have none. A single encoder layer, however, is smaller than the embedding layer.

questions.question: Can you name three downstream tasks that the same backbone could serve, and say how each would use the per-token outputs?
questions.answer: Sentence classification (pool, then Dense), span identification (per-token start/end scores), part-of-speech tagging (per-token class).
questions.explanation: These are the three examples in p481_e03; the head determines how the features are used.
